description:
We are Lunarmartians, a team passionate about space exploration, science, technology, and discovering the mysteries of the Moon and Mars. Our goal is to explore new ideas, solve problems creatively, and learn more about the possibilities of human exploration beyond Earth.

We believe in teamwork, curiosity, innovation, and sharing knowledge. We welcome members who are enthusiastic, willing to learn, and ready to contribute their ideas and skills.
summary:
Abandoned but not Forgotten is a digital storytelling booklet that maps the human-made objects left behind on the Moon and Mars: lunar module descent stages, rovers, landers, scientific packages and deliberate impact sites — the hardware of missions that ended but never came home.

We built it using NASA’s open data. The NSSDCA Table of Anthropogenic Impacts and Spacecraft on the Moon and the NASA History Office Catalogue of Manmade Material on the Moon gave us the inventory and coordinates; LROC imagery provided orbital views of the Apollo sites, where the Lunar Module descent stage, ALSEP package and Surveyor III are still visible alongside astronaut tracks; HiRISE imagery documented Opportunity’s lander and discarded landing hardware on Mars.

Each object is presented with its location, its mission story and its present condition, turning scattered coordinate tables into a narrative that a general audience can follow.

This matters because these objects are humanity’s first material heritage beyond Earth. As the Moon becomes more accessible to national programmes and private companies, protecting these artefacts depends first on knowing what is there and where — and on the public caring that it exists.
details:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is a digital booklet about the human-made objects left behind on the Moon and Mars. NASA’s archives record them as observation IDs and technical captions. I found the orbital images that show these objects still sitting on the surface and rewrote the record as a story — what each one did, how it got there, and why it was left.

The aim is simple: these sites can only be protected if people know they exist. As the Moon gets busier with national and private missions, a booklet a student or policymaker can read in ten minutes does more for that than an archive of image identifiers.

Tools — no code. Research came from LROC, whose low-altitude images of the Apollo sites show the Lunar Module descent stages, the deployed surface experiment packages and Surveyor III alongside astronaut tracks; HiRISE, which imaged Opportunity’s lander in Eagle Crater with the backshell, parachute and heat shield; the NSSDCA catalogue of objects left on other worlds; and the UN Register of Objects Launched into Outer Space. Canva handled layout and the image plates, exported as a PDF. Heyzine publishes that PDF as a flip-book that opens in any browser with no app or login. ChatGPT and Claude supported research and drafting, with every factual claim checked against the original source.

What makes it creative: most orbital-imagery projects produce a map or a dashboard. I made a memorial instead — the objects treated as artefacts with biographies rather than data points.

Factors considered: accessibility (readable on a phone, nothing to install), accuracy (primary mission imagery, never claiming an object is visible where it isn’t), licensing (HiRISE images are public domain, credit line included), the limits of my sources (the UN Register lists missions, not debris), and scope (Moon and Mars only, not Earth orbit).
dataRefs: NSSDCA – Table of Anthropogenic Impacts and Spacecraft on the Moon
LROC – Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (Arizona State University)
HiRISE – Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (University of Arizona)
NASA – Human Artifacts on the Moon (Artifact Maps)
